_readme: Hand-written notes shown when an Iconic discovery is collected.
Every line must be checkable against the plaque inscription or be a fact so
well established it is not in dispute. Nothing is generated, and nothing is
asserted about a real person that the record does not support. Plaques with
no entry here fall back to facts derived from the dataset itself, so this
file can stay short and stay honest. Keyed by OpenPlaques plaque id.
595: He lived at number 23. Handel had lived at number 25, two hundred years earlier — the only pair of neighbours in London separated by that much time.
41802: He grew up in this house as Farrokh Bulsara, a long way from Wembley Stadium.
381: The man who broke Enigma was born here. He never lived to see the machines he described.
599: She wrote what is now considered the first computer program — a century before there was a computer to run it.
431: She had begun Frankenstein at eighteen. She was fifty-three when she moved here.
42876: He arrived in Flat 15 as a music hall performer. Within a decade he was the most recognised person alive.
52362: He lived here in 1977, the year Exodus came out — recorded in London while he recovered from being shot in Kingston.
79: He fled Vienna in 1938 with the Gestapo at his back, and died here the following year.
559: He lived on this site while writing up the Beagle voyage — twenty years before he dared publish what it had led him to think.
178: The best-selling novelist in history lived here while writing some of her most famous cases.
287: He was at the height of his fame when he lived here, and had lost everything within five years of leaving.
1105: He lived here in two rooms with his family, in real poverty, while writing in the British Museum reading room.
6: She lived and died on this site — and did more for public health with statistics than most do with medicine.
55764: The Muppets were made in Britain, and the man who made them lived on this hill.
189: Eric Blair lived here. George Orwell was the name he published under.
337: He lived in this house for thirty-six years and died in it — the only London address he ever really had.
